intro: The investigation was undertaken to establish how the district of production, the length of post-harvest storage and the method of processing govern the quality of the traditional aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal, and to identify the cultivar and product combinations best suited to each end use. The summary and the conclusion of each of the three experiments are presented below, followed by the overall conclusion of the investigation.
S1a: Experiment I examined the grain quality of three traditional aromatic landraces of West Bengal, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira, grown at Nadia, Purba Bardhaman and Birbhum/Howrah and sampled as fresh paddy and again at 4, 8 and 12 months after harvest. The trial followed a factorial randomised block design with three replications, was repeated over two years and covered thirty-eight parameters. The effect of location was significant for all twenty-three parameters in which storage was assayed, the effect of variety for all twenty-three and the effect of storage for nineteen. Nadia returned the highest hulling (77.02%), soluble protein, fat, copper and zinc together with the lowest phytic acid; Birbhum and Howrah the highest milling percentage, head rice recovery, total phenol, total flavonoid, antioxidant capacity, iron and aroma; and Purba Bardhaman proved the weakest location for most characters determining nutritional value, although it returned the highest amylose and the brightest grain. Kalojira emerged as the superior all-round landrace, leading for hulling, milling, head rice recovery, total starch, amylose, fat, ash, aroma, total phenol, total flavonoid and antioxidant capacity, while Gobindabhog was superior for soluble protein, grain shape, iron and thirteen of the fifteen amino acids, and Radhunipagal ranked highest for zinc alone.
S1b: Storage displaced quality in two opposing directions simultaneously. Head rice recovery gained 2.13 percentage points up to eight months and amylose rose by 12.8% over the year, whereas aroma declined by 31.7%, soluble protein by 41.4%, fat by 31.3%, total phenol by 52.4%, total flavonoid by 37.3% and antioxidant capacity by 62.7%. Copper, iron, zinc and manganese registered no change during storage while phytic acid declined by 40.0%, so that the phytate to mineral ratio improved with ageing and aged grain should release its micronutrients more readily than fresh grain despite containing no greater quantity of them. The interactions yielded three inferences that the main effects alone would conceal. For the milling characters and for aroma the order of the landraces held at every location, so that the choice of landrace may be made once for the whole of South Bengal. For soluble protein, ash and the four minerals the order changed with location, so that no recommendation can be advanced for these characters without naming the district. For aroma, fat and amylose all three landraces changed at nearly identical rates, so that a single storage regime will serve them all. Cluster analysis separated the twelve Kalojira treatments as a single group before any other division appeared in the tree.
C1: The quality of these landraces is governed jointly by genotype, growing location and storage period, the three acting in conjunction rather than independently, so that any recommendation naming only the cultivar is incomplete. Kalojira is the superior all-round choice, combining the best milling outturn with the highest aroma and the greatest phenolic and antioxidant content, while Gobindabhog is the appropriate selection where protein quality or grain iron outweighs aroma. Storage improves milling behaviour and reduces phytic acid, but at the cost of severe and irreversible losses of aroma, extractable protein, lipid and antioxidant capacity. A holding period of four to eight months reconciles these opposing trends, since within that window the greater part of the milling gain conferred by ageing has been realised while the loss of the health-promoting fractions remains moderate. Where protracted holding is unavoidable, cool storage merits consideration, since temperature rather than time governs the rate of these losses. The desirable attributes of these landraces, namely aroma, lipid, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant capacity and soluble protein, constitute a single tightly associated complex that declines in concert and cannot be recovered once lost. The premium these rices command therefore rests upon the attributes most rapidly forfeited in store, and its realisation depends upon the marketing chain as much as upon the breeding programme.
S2a: Experiment II evaluated seven traditional products prepared from nine aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal together with Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar serving as the control. Four of the products were cooked, namely table rice, khichdi, pulao and payash, and three were processed, namely popped rice, puffed rice and flattened rice. Each was laid out in a completely randomised design with three replications and repeated over two years, the two years being analysed jointly as a pooled design, and between twenty-two and twenty-five quality attributes were determined in each product, covering the nutritional, bioactive, mineral, colour and sensory groups. Across the seven products the cultivars differed significantly for nearly every attribute determined, whereas the year of production and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. This margin constitutes the central result of the experiment: almost every attribute separated the cultivars, while far fewer separated the years or exhibited any change in the magnitude of the cultivar differences between years. The identity of the cultivar therefore governs the quality of the finished product, the year in which the crop was grown is of markedly less consequence, and a cultivar selected on one year of data may be expected to retain its position in the next.
S2b: A composite quality score index was constructed by the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), each attribute being scored from 0 to 100 in the favourable direction, averaged within five groups and combined by weight, sensory carrying 30 per cent, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. On this index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice (64.5), Radhunipagal for khichdi (69.1), Kataribhog for pulao (70.1), Gobindabhog for payash (77.9) and for popped rice (64.5), Radhatilak for puffed rice (62.9) and Harinakhuri for flattened rice (65.8). The non-aromatic control ranked at or near the bottom of the order in every product, so that the margin available to a processor who changes only the raw material is substantial. Weights derived independently from principal component analysis reproduced the same ranking, with a mean Spearman rank correlation of 0.946 and the same leading cultivar in six of the seven products, so that the ranking is a property of the data and not of the weighting convention adopted. Cluster analysis of the cultivar and product combinations yielded seven groups, five of which contained a single product only.
C2: The quality of these seven traditional products is determined principally by the cultivar from which they are prepared. For each product a specific cultivar may be recommended: Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice, Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice. No single cultivar was superior for all seven products, so that the choice of raw material must follow the product intended; where a processor prepares more than one of them, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Kalonunia and Radhatilak perform well across the widest range. The non-aromatic control ranked at or near the bottom in every product, and substituting the cultivars named here for it would raise the quality of every preparation appreciably, without any alteration in the method of preparation. The clustering indicates that when one preparation is compared with another it is the method of preparation, not the cultivar, that determines the broad quality type, whereas within any one preparation the cultivar is the variable under the processor's control. The preparation therefore fixes the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type. The index ranks these ten entries relative to one another and would require recomputation were further cultivars added.
S3a: Experiment III evaluated the sensory and nutritional quality of idli prepared from three aromatic landraces, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira, together with the non-aromatic check Dudeshwar, each used plain and fortified with carrot or beet extract. The experiment followed a two-factor completely randomised design with three replications, was repeated in two consecutive years and yielded twelve treatment combinations and forty two quality parameters. Pooling was justified by the Bartlett chi-square test, which proved non-significant for all but four characters. The variety and product interaction was highly significant for most of the nutritional, mineral, colour and textural characters, proving non-significant only for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability. Amylose declined from 16.75 per cent in DI to 9.78 per cent in RBI, starch from 51.66 to 24.05 per cent and total carbohydrate from 60.21 to 40.91 per cent, while total soluble sugar rose from 0.53 per cent in RI to 3.83 per cent in RBI. Resistant starch was highest in DCI at 1.97 per cent, and the predicted glycaemic index lowest in RCI at 58.46 and highest in KBI at 75.08. Total protein ranged from 13.44 per cent in KI to 10.92 per cent in DCI, the three aromatic landraces exceeding the check throughout.
S3b: The bioactive fractions exhibited the widest variation of any group of characters. Total phenol ranged from 290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in KBI to 53.47 in DI, a differential exceeding fivefold, with total flavonoid from 171.34 to 42.95 mg QE 100 g⁻¹ and total antioxidant activity from 426.88 to 165.26 mg TE 100 g⁻¹ following the same order. Beta-carotene was contributed almost entirely by carrot, attaining 45.77 in KCI against nil in every plain treatment, while anthocyanin was recorded only in the beet fortified treatments, attaining 1.86 in KBI. Calcium exhibited the greatest response to fortification, rising from 61.44 mg L⁻¹ in KI to 550.88 in GBI, although phytate rose in parallel from 0.82 mg g⁻¹ in GI to 2.52 in KBI. Fortification lowered lightness from 72.92 in DI to 36.47 in DBI and softened the product, hardness declining from 147.73 in KI to 45.09 in DI. Aroma was scored highest in GI at 7.70 and lowest in KCI at 5.65, whereas for every other sensory attribute the fortified treatments were superior, overall acceptability ranging from 8.64 in KBI to 6.14 in DI. The non-significant interaction for the principal sensory attributes established that the benefit conferred by fortification was of equal magnitude in all four varieties.
C3: Variety, type of fortification and their interaction all exert a significant influence upon the quality of idli prepared from aromatic rice, fortification proving the stronger of the two factors. Both the principal component analysis and the cluster analysis identified fortification, rather than variety, as the principal source of variation in product quality. The three aromatic landraces were superior to the non-aromatic check for protein, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant potential and every sensory attribute examined, which affords a nutritional justification, in addition to the cultural and aromatic value already recognised, for the continued cultivation and conservation of these landraces. Beetroot-fortified Kalojira idli is recommended as the superior overall combination, returning the highest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, soluble protein, anthocyanin and overall acceptability. The carrot-fortified product is indicated where a provitamin A-rich preparation of low glycaemic response is required, and beet-fortified Gobindabhog where a mineral-enriched product is required. The mineral gain is partly offset by the accompanying rise in phytate, so that the phytate to mineral ratio rather than the mineral content alone should be used in judging nutritional value. Enrichment with carrot or beetroot extract improves nutritional and sensory quality without recourse to any synthetic colour or additive, and offers a practical route to a functional fermented food built upon indigenous aromatic germplasm.
OC: Taken together, the three experiments establish that the quality of the traditional aromatic rice of West Bengal is not a fixed property of the landrace. It is determined jointly by the genotype, the district in which the crop is raised, the period for which the paddy is held and the preparation for which the grain is finally used, so that any recommendation naming only the cultivar is incomplete. For grain quality, Kalojira grown at Nadia and used within eight months of harvest gives the best overall result, while Gobindabhog is the choice where protein and amino acid quality matter more than aroma. For value addition the cultivar must be matched to the product, Gobindabhog serving best for payash and popped rice, Kalojira for table rice and for fermented idli, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice. Enrichment of idli with carrot or beetroot extract improves its nutritional and sensory quality without any synthetic additive. The location-specific quality data generated here for four Geographical Indication protected landraces, Gobindabhog, Tulaipanji, Kalonunia and Radhunipagal, provide an objective basis for authentication, for the fixing of safe storage periods and for the market development of the traditional aromatic rice of West Bengal.
